cancer-mediated hypercoagulable states are associated with enhanced fibrinolyic susceptibility to tPA.
the hypercoagulable state of plasma from cancer patients is diminished by enhanced fibrilolytic activity, as measured in vitro using thrombelastography and exogenous tPA.
patients with breast, colon/pancreatic or lung cancers have enhanced fibrinolytisic vulnerability to tissue plasminogen activation compared to normal individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of thrombosis and fibrinolysis as they relate to cancer.
the effects of cancer on the coagulation system.
the role played by cancer-mediated changes in coagulation in the development of thrombotic events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cancer-associated fibrinolysis was not hypofibrinolysis but was enhanced hyperfibrinolysis.
the hypercoagulable state in patients with cancer is in part counterbalanced by an increase in tPA-mediated fibrinolysis.
the hypercoagulable states that occur with cancer are not due to hypofibrinolysis, and that cancer-associated fibrinolysis appears to be enhanced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cancer-associated hypercoagulable state is not a simple one, but rather is a complex interaction between pro- and anticoagulant proteins.
cancer-mediated alterations in hemostasis result in a hypercoagulable state, but that this hypercoagulopathy is in part offset by enhanced fibrinolysis.
cancer-mediated hypercoagulation is not a result of a hypofibrino-lytic state, but rather is the product of enhanced hypercoagulation that is partially offset by enhanced fibrinolysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cancer-associated hypercoagulable states are not simply a function of hypercoagulopathy.
cancer patients are not hypofibrinolitic, but are hyperfibrinolytic, and this is a compensatory response to the hypercoagulation that is associated with cancer.
cancer-associated changes in hemostasis are not as simple as cancer-mediated changes in coagulation promoting hypercoagulation.
